🇲🇽🚆 <u>PROFEPA IS SITTING ON 70 TREN MAYA ENVIRONMENTAL FILES — SOME STRETCHED TO THE 5-YEAR LIMIT</u>

A Contralínea investigation finds Mexico's environmental enforcement agency, Profepa, holding 70 open inspection files tied to the Tren Maya — 24 of them on the main rail sections — and dragging some out to the maximum five years without resolution, including damage to 8 cenotes and caves in Section 5. Profepa insists it "is not obstructing anything related to the project." The railway is running; the remediation isn't.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>NO POST FOR AN ABUSER: SENER WON'T SEAT EX-PEMEX CHIEF AFTER VIDEO OF HIM BEATING HIS WIFE</u>

Mexico's Energy Ministry confirmed it will not formalize Víctor Rodríguez Padilla — former director of Pemex — as head of the National Institute of Electricity and Clean Energy (INEEL), after his wife María Felicia Jiménez released a five-minute video of him assaulting her. He had already been presented in the role on June 1; now Sener says the appointment was never formalized and won't be. President Sheinbaum pledged to support the victim directly. No title shields anyone from accountability.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>MEXICO AND US OPEN BINATIONAL SCREWWORM PLANT — AND WASHINGTON IS FUNDING IT ON MEXICAN SOIL</u>

In Metapa, Chiapas, President Sheinbaum and US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins reopened a binational sterile-fly plant that will breed 100 million flies a week to stop the screwworm at Mexico's southern border. The plant cost $61 million jointly — and Washington just pledged $83.8 million more to scale up production inside Mexico. Rollins called Sheinbaum "an extraordinary partner": the foreign power funding a plant on Mexican soil, not the other way around.
📸 Plan Nacional de Maíz Nativo — Pijijiapan, Chiapas · 27 de junio de 2026

🇲🇽✊ A guaranteed price so the people who grow the corn can live from their work. "The campesino, the campesina who plants corn should be able to live from their labor — enough for self-consumption, for the family." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Pijijiapan, Chiapas This season Mexico set a guaranteed price near 7,200 pesos per ton, cutting out the middlemen who long underpaid small growers. Gov. Eduardo Ramírez thanked the program for ending the coyote that exploited Chiapas farmers.

🇲🇽🎨 "We come from corn. We were made from corn." "That is the depth of the bond between every Indigenous people — and all 130 million Mexicans — and corn." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Pijijiapan, Chiapas The Popol Vuh, the Maya book of creation, tells that the first humans were formed from maize. Sheinbaum invoked it while defending Mexico's native corn — domesticated from wild teosinte by ancient peoples over 8,000 years.

🇲🇽✊ "If we lost native corn, we would lose a good part of our food sovereignty — of what we are as Mexican women and men." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Pijijiapan, Chiapas Mexico safeguards 54 native corn varieties; 29 of them grow in Chiapas alone. Sheinbaum launched the national stage of 'El Maíz es la Raíz,' now reaching 270,000 farmers across 8 states. Hybrid seed must be bought every year and can't be replanted — native seed keeps the land, and the country, sovereign.

🇲🇽🐉🌐 Mexico is where the US-China tariff war gets built

General Motors is relocating production of two China-built models — the Chevrolet Aveo and the Groove — to its Ramos Arizpe complex in Coahuila, with assembly starting in 2027 and a target of 80,000 units a year by 2030. It's part of the $1 billion GM committed to its Mexican operations back in January.

The logic is pure geography of sovereignty. Mexico now charges 50% on cars from countries with no trade deal — China included — while the US slaps 25% on Mexican-built vehicles. Assembling in Mexico vaults both walls at once. GM's Chinese joint venture currently ships about 130,000 vehicles a year into Mexico; that flow is being onshored.

Tariff walls don't erase production — they relocate it. And when Washington and Beijing both raise barriers, the factory address that makes sense to both sides is Mexico. Not a vassal in someone else's trade war — the ground it gets fought on. 🇲🇽

🇲🇽🐉 Mexico won't rush the USMCA review just to please Washington

The July 1 deadline lands this week — and Washington itself now projects the review will run past it. After a second bilateral round in June on agriculture and energy, a third round is set for the week of July 20 in Mexico City. No signatures forced by a calendar.

The US is pushing stricter rules of origin to wall Chinese content out of North American supply chains. Mexico has already moved on its own terms: tariffs on more than 1,400 products from non-FTA countries, plus 52 US trade demands on the table. But Ebrard's message is "no rush" — Mexico won't accept terms that compromise the national interest just to hit a date.

That's the sovereign read. China sells Mexico roughly $130B a year — much of it intermediate goods Mexican plants turn into exports — against about $10B flowing back. Diversification isn't picking a side; it's refusing to let any partner set your clock. 🇲🇽

🇲🇽🌎 "Our relationship with the United States must be built on recognition of each nation's sovereignty." "Nuestra relación con los Estados Unidos debe seguir construyéndose sobre principios muy claros: el respeto mutuo, el diálogo, la cooperación, y el reconocimiento de la soberanía de cada nación." "Our relationship with the United States must keep being built on very clear principles: mutual respect, dialogue, cooperation, and recognition of each nation's sovereignty." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, Metapa, Chiapas Said with US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and US Ambassador Ronald Johnson present. The plant targets the screwworm, a pest that crosses borders. As Sheinbaum put it: animal diseases and plagues "know no borders" — the answer is shared capacity, not confrontation.
